extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a letter to the editor with limited data reporting. Key tables (S1–S5) are in supplementary materials and not available in the provided text, so per-arm baseline demographics and per-arm event counts for each outcome are not extractable. The total nondeceased analyzed sample is n=634 (647 followed minus 13 deaths), split 178 Paxlovid vs 456 no-Paxlovid. Percent female calculated as 345/634=54.4%. The continuous CAT score association (outcome_id 3) was assessed by multiple linear regression but no effect size or CI values were provided in the text. All-cause mortality analysis used 1:4 PSM matching 65 patients total, but no OR/HR with CI was reported in the letter text. Unadjusted OR for Long COVID (Paxlovid vs. no Paxlovid): 0.316 (95% CI 0.188–0.531, p<0.001) from univariate logistic analysis also extractable from Table 1. Individual sequelae (cough, fatigue, expectoration, etc.) reported in Table S2 but not available in the provided text.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an observational retrospective cohort study examining NMV-r for PREVENTION of PASC during acute COVID-19, not treatment of existing PASC. The abstract contains minor discrepancies in CI reporting between abstract (0.76-0.82 for broadly defined PASC 30-90d) and results text (0.77-0.83) and tables (0.767-0.827); table values used as most granular. summary: This retrospective cohort study examined the short- and long-term effectiveness of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir versus molnupiravir in 1,745 Hong Kong asthma patients infected with COVID-19 (Omicron era), using SMR weighting to adjust for confounding. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with significantly reduced risks of acute mortality (HR 0.27), post-acute mortality (HR 0.49), all-cause post-acute hospitalization (HR 0.72), and myocardial infarction (HR 0.10) versus no antiviral; molnupiravir reduced only acute mortality versus no antiviral. Head-to-head comparison showed nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was superior to molnupiravir for post-acute all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.65, p<0.001) and asthma exacerbation in moderate-to-severe asthma patients, suggesting nirmatrelvir/ritonavir offers broader post-acute protection in the asthma population.

summary: This retrospective population-based cohort study of 188,532 Singaporeans aged ≥60 years with SARS-CoV-2 infection examined whether early outpatient nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment (n=10,905) reduced risk of postacute sequelae compared to untreated controls (n=177,627), using overlap-weighted competing-risks regression on national registry and claims data. No statistically significant reduction in any prespecified postacute outcome was observed at 31–180 days post-infection, including composite sequelae (aHR 1.06; 95% CI 0.94–1.19), MACE (aHR 0.80; 0.61–1.06), cardiovascular, neurological, respiratory, or autoimmune complications, or any symptom-based sequelae (aHR 0.97; 0.80–1.18). The authors attribute the null finding largely to a highly vaccinated/boosted cohort (95% with ≥3 doses) and a very low hospitalization rate (<2%), which may have left little additional benefit for antivirals to confer.

summary: This paper is a descriptive demographic analysis of the PAX LC trial — a Phase 2 decentralized, double-blind, 1:1 randomized placebo-controlled trial of 15-day nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) vs placebo/ritonavir in 100 highly symptomatic community-dwelling adults with long COVID across 48 US states. The paper does not report clinical outcomes or efficacy data; it compares the trial's enrolled demographic profile to the 2023 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) long COVID population. Key findings were that the PAX LC cohort was younger (median 42 vs 53 years), similarly female (66% both groups), but substantially more Non-Hispanic White (89% vs 61%) and underrepresented in Hispanic (5% vs 20%) and Non-Hispanic Black (1% vs 12%) participants compared to NHIS.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper contains NO clinical outcome data — it is purely a demographic characterization and representativeness analysis of PAX LC trial enrollment compared to NHIS. No per-arm data, no efficacy endpoints, no adverse events, and no between-group effect estimates are reported. The trial itself (NCT05668091) tests nirmatrelvir/ritonavir for long COVID; efficacy results would be in a separate publication. Age is reported as median/IQR for the overall trial cohort only (not per arm). Per-arm sample sizes (1:1 randomization implies ~50 per arm) are not explicitly stated. The ~1000 figure for screened participants is inferred from 'more than 1000 individuals to access the prescreening questions' with 'approximately one-third passing the prescreening stage.' The 15-day treatment duration is explicitly stated.

summary: This EHR-based target trial emulation used the N3C database (445,738 patients with COVID-19 eligible for Paxlovid from April 2022-February 2023) to estimate whether Paxlovid treatment during acute COVID-19 prevents long COVID (PASC) onset. Paxlovid had no significant effect on overall PASC incidence (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.02) or respiratory symptoms, but showed small statistically significant protective effects on incident cognitive (RR 0.91) and fatigue (RR 0.94) symptoms. Stratified analyses identified small protective effects in patients aged ≥65 years (RR 0.92, NNT 233) and with CCI 3-4 (RR 0.83, NNT 76), but the authors conclude Paxlovid is unlikely to be a definitive solution for PASC prevention given the negligible absolute effect sizes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a PASC prevention study (Paxlovid given during acute COVID-19), NOT a treatment study for established long COVID. Study period: April 1, 2022 to February 28, 2023 (mostly Omicron BA and later subvariants). The pooled sequential trial cohort of 460,803 records differs from the 445,738 unique patients due to sequential trial design allowing some patients to appear in both treatment and control groups across different trials. Age data reported only as distributional bins (not means/SDs). Cumulative incidence values in Table 3 are reported as proportions (e.g., 0.045 = 4.5%). Death counts: Paxlovid arm 157 deaths (29-180 days), 51 deaths (1-28 days); control arm 609 deaths (29-180 days), 366 deaths (1-28 days). Extensive sensitivity analyses (14 variations) all confirm null primary result — see Table 3. Also note: the paper reports adjusted cumulative incidence estimates (4.53% treated, 4.60% untreated) in text but the raw (unadjusted) event counts show 4.4% treated vs 4.1% untreated, reflecting the IPTW adjustment. Vaccination subanalysis: 115,823 patients, 8 sites, 79.15% fully vaccinated, 45.67% treated. Doubly robust adjustment gave HR 0.983 (95% CI 0.950-1.018, p=0.305).

summary: This large observational cohort study using target trial emulation analyzed 497,499 SARS-CoV-2-infected adults from 29 US PCORnet EHR repositories to assess whether nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) prescribed within 5 days of infection reduces Long COVID risk. Among high-risk non-hospitalized adults (n=431,707 analyzed), Paxlovid was associated with significantly reduced incidence of Long COVID (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.87-0.89; absolute risk reduction 2.99 events/100 persons), all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.70), and death (HR 0.53) in the 30-180 day post-acute period. No significant Long COVID risk reduction was observed in low-risk patients (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.95-1.11), suggesting Paxlovid's preventive benefit for Long COVID is limited to high-risk individuals.

summary: This single-center retrospective cohort study in China enrolled 372 hospitalized patients with post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis (PCPF), comparing 293 who received nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (SMADs) during acute infection to 79 who did not, with 1-year follow-up. Among survivors with follow-up data, the SMAD group had a significantly lower 1-year readmission rate (45.97% vs. 63.64%, p=0.020; HR=0.65, 95% CI 0.44-0.96, p=0.030) and lower in-hospital mortality (3.07% vs. 8.86%, p=0.024; adjusted OR=0.31, 95% CI 0.11-0.86). SMAD treatment was not significantly associated with 1-year post-discharge mortality (HR=0.51, 95% CI 0.25-1.03, p=0.059), and CT scores at 12 months were significantly lower in the SMAD group, suggesting antiviral therapy during acute COVID-19 may reduce long-term pulmonary fibrosis progression.

summary: This retrospective EHR cohort study examined whether acute nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment reduces long COVID risk in 2,740 immunodeficient patients (597 with primary IEI, 2,143 with secondary/other immunodeficiency) at a single US center. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a conference abstract (P367) embedded in a multi-abstract proceedings document. The paper text also contains fragments from adjacent abstracts (P366, P368, P369, P370) which were excluded from extraction. No formal randomization described — this appears to be a controlled but non-randomized study. Within-group p-values reported (Group A: p<0.0001; Group B: p<0.021) but no between-group statistical comparison provided; between-group mean difference at 3 months calculated as 419-332=87m. The paper_id assigned corresponds to the proceedings DOI prefix; the exact abstract identifier for P367 is not confirmed.

summary: This paper (abstract P367) tested oral L-arginine plus liposomal vitamin C (Bioarginina VRC, 1.66g twice daily) versus standard treatment in 80 post-COVID-19 patients with high cardiovascular risk undergoing cardiac rehabilitation over 90 days. The primary outcome was six-minute walk test (6MWT) distance: the supplemented group improved from 289m to 419m (+130m), while the control group improved from 280m to 332m (+52m), with both changes statistically significant. No safety concerns were reported, but the study lacks randomization details and the control group was smaller (30 vs 50 patients), limiting conclusions about the supplement's independent effect beyond rehabilitation alone.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved by 130m in the supplemented group (289 to 419m, p<0.0001) vs 52m in controls (280 to 332m, p=0.021), a between-group difference of ~78m.

domains.support: The study describes itself as an analysis of 'routine data' with no mention of randomization. Patients were non-randomly allocated to groups based on clinical decision. No randomization sequence, allocation concealment, or CONSORT flow diagram is described.
The study is open-label with no blinding of participants or clinicians. Both groups received cardiac rehabilitation; adherence monitoring not reported. No intention-to-treat analysis described.
No attrition or dropout data are reported. The same N (50 and 30) appears at baseline and follow-up, suggesting either complete follow-up or that dropouts are not described.
Outcomes (6MWT, Borg scale, EQ-5D) are measured by nurses/clinicians without blinding. Validated instruments used, but open-label design risks performance bias especially for subjective measures.
No trial registration or pre-specified analysis plan is mentioned. Multiple outcomes reported selectively with no correction for multiple comparisons.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study is described as a retrospective analysis of routine data, NOT an RCT; design_type was set to quasi-experimental accordingly. No randomization is described. Table 2 for BRPE has duplicated rows due to PDF parsing; baseline SD for Group B BRPE is split across rows (3.28 and 2.94 appear as separate lines — interpreted as mean=3.28, SD=2.94 per the table structure). The LVEF column in Table 3 shows baseline values for Group A=52±7 and Group B=51±7; after 3 months Group A=53±4 and Group B=51±2 — note the p-value of 0.17 is listed in the baseline column and 0.02 in the follow-up column, suggesting the between-group comparison at follow-up reached significance. Table 5 (EQ-5D) spans two page segments due to PDF formatting; the bottom portion including EQ5D-VAS was parsed from a separate table fragment. Echocardiographic parameters left ventricular diastolic dimension, septal thickness, posterior wall thickness, left atrial size, right ventricular basal diameter, and pulmonary artery systolic pressure are reported in Table 3 but excluded from outcomes extraction to stay within size limits; all showed no significant between-group differences. Laboratory results (glucose, creatinine, BUN, sodium, potassium, hemoglobin, AST, ALT) from Table 4 were omitted from outcomes for the same reason; all showed no significant between-group differences. EQ-5D moderate and extreme pain/discomfort, moderate/extreme anxiety/depression, some problems/confined to bed for mobility, and unable to perform usual activities subcategories were omitted from outcomes but all raw counts are in Table 5 in the paper. Within-group p-values: Group A 6MWT p<0.0001; Group B 6MWT p<0.021; Group A BRPE p=0.048; Group B BRPE p=0.246. No between-group p-values for 6MWT or BRPE were explicitly reported; between-group effects calculated from per-arm endpoint means.

summary: This study tested oral L-arginine plus liposomal vitamin C (Bioarginina C, 3.32 g/day) versus standard treatment alone in 80 high-cardiovascular-risk long COVID patients undergoing cardiac rehabilitation over 3 months. The primary outcome was functional capacity measured by the six-minute walk test (6MWT): the supplemented group improved by 130 m (289 m to 419 m, p<0.0001) compared to 52 m in controls (280 m to 332 m, p=0.021), with perceived exertion improving significantly only in the supplemented group (Borg score 3.44 to 2.46, p=0.048 vs. non-significant in controls). Quality-of-life scores on the EQ-5D-VAS also favoured the supplemented group after 3 months (77 vs. 70, p=0.032), with no significant differences in echocardiographic or laboratory safety parameters between groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved by 130 m in the supplemented group vs. 52 m in controls (419 m vs. 332 m at 3 months); between-group difference not formally reported but within-group p<0.0001 vs. p=0.021.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study reports IPTW-adjusted risk ratios for the composite and 16 individual Long COVID outcomes. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Individual HR and 95% CI values for the 13 individual post-acute sequelae (outcomes 5-12 and ischemic heart disease, diabetes, dysautonomia, shortness of breath, cough) are reported only in Figure 3 — exact numerical values are not stated in the text or tables. Only the directional finding is stated verbatim (molnupiravir associated with reduced risk of 8/13 sequelae; not statistically significant for ischemic heart disease, diabetes, dysautonomia, shortness of breath, cough). Per-arm event counts for individual sequelae are not reported. The PASC score is not a traditional clinical outcome scale but a composite weighted burden metric. This is a prevention study (treatment given during acute COVID-19 to prevent long COVID), not a treatment study of established long COVID. The study population is veterans (>91% male, predominantly older, US-based), limiting generalizability. The paper is an observational cohort study using IPTW, not an RCT.

summary: This prospective open-label matched-controlled observational study evaluated Actovegin (deproteinized calf blood hemodialysate) versus no Actovegin in 440 post-COVID-19 patients with chronic cerebral ischaemia (CCI) in Russia (n=220 per arm), followed for 90 days. At 90 days, the Actovegin group had significantly lower symptom frequency (38.5% vs 62.1%, p<0.01), greater improvement in fatigue (MFI-20 mean 48 vs 61), sleep (Spiegel SSQ 22 vs 17), and cognition (MoCA +4 vs +1 points), and higher rates of no/minimal quality of life impairment (77.9% vs 33.7%, p<0.001). All between-group differences were statistically significant (p<0.05), though the open-label non-randomized design limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Paper is in Russian with English abstract; all numeric data extracted from figures (Fig 2, 3, 4) and tables. No SDs reported for any continuous outcome — only mean scores at each timepoint from figures. Between-group p-values stated as thresholds only (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001), not exact values. Baseline MFI-20 scores from Fig 2: arm1=69, arm2=66; Day30: arm1=51, arm2=57; Day90: arm1=48, arm2=61. The paper states arm1 decreased 18 pts at Day30 and arm2 decreased 9 pts, which is consistent with 69→51 and 66→57 respectively. MMSE Table 2 reports distribution by severity at Day90 (endpoint only, no baseline severity distribution given separately). Table 3 (MMSE subscores) and Table 4 (MoCA subscores) report % of patients with improvement per cognitive domain — these are proportions of the subgroup who had that impairment at baseline, not of total n=220. Denominators for Tables 3 and 4 are the number impaired at baseline per domain (from Table 1). Depression severity distribution (Table 5) denominator for severity breakdown is among those with depression: arm1 n=69, arm2 n=106. Anxiety distribution (Table 6) is for full n=220 per arm. MoCA baseline arm1=21, arm2=20 from Fig 4 (paper says overall mean ~20-21). Note: paper explicitly states observational design without randomization or placebo control as a limitation.

summary: This retrospective cohort study used N3C electronic health record data from 74 US institutions (October 2021–April 2023) to compare incident PASC risk among T2DM adults on prevalent monotherapy metformin (n=5,596) versus sulfonylurea or DPP-4 inhibitor (n=1,451), using entropy balancing for confounding control. In the weighted analysis with ICD-10-defined PASC, 3-month and 6-month risk ratios were 0.86 (95% CI 0.56–1.32) and 0.81 (95% CI 0.55–1.20), respectively — directionally consistent with benefit but not statistically significant. The authors conclude that the results are compatible with a reduced PASC risk with metformin but that wide confidence intervals and methodological limitations (prevalent-user design, non-specific outcome definition) preclude causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study uses two cohorts: cohort one (n=7,047; 29 sites) for ICD-10-defined PASC outcome; cohort two (n=13,824; 37 sites) for ML-predicted probability outcome. ML outcome arm-level means (0.33 SD 0.14 at 3 months; 0.42 SD 0.16 at 6 months) are reported as overall cohort two means, not separately by arm — per-arm means for ML outcome are not available verbatim. The 'percent female 56%' stated in abstract refers to overall cohort; arm-level percent female is calculated as 100 minus percent male (44.0% male in metformin arm, 45.9% male in SU/DPP4i arm). Risk difference for 3-month ICD-10 outcome in abstract states -3.06 per 1000 (approx -0.31 per 100) which matches Table 4; similarly 6-month RD -4.91 per 1000 ≈ -0.49 per 100. Sensitivity analysis results referenced in Supplemental Figure 2 and Supplemental Tables 2 and 3 — not available in this text. Log BMI reported (mean 3.5, SD 0.3/0.2) rather than raw BMI.

summary: This single-center retrospective cohort study examined 54 adults with post-acute COVID-19 VTE (PE or DVT within 90 days of infection) at a Romanian tertiary hospital between 2020-2022, comparing 11 patients who received systemic thrombolysis to 43 managed conservatively. Thrombolysis recipients had markedly lower TAPSE (13.0 vs. 20.8 mm), lower SpO2 (90.1% vs. 97.0%), and smaller LVEDD (24.4 vs. 46.1 mm), all statistically significant; in multivariable regression, each 1 mm decrease in TAPSE (OR 1.58) and each 1% decrease in SpO2 (OR 1.34) independently predicted thrombolysis. Inflammatory biomarkers (CRP, fibrinogen) and RV diameter were not associated with treatment group, supporting a non-invasive hemodynamic triad (low TAPSE, low SpO2, reduced LVEDD) as bedside risk-stratification markers for post-COVID VTE.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective cohort study using thrombolysis vs. no thrombolysis as a de facto two-arm comparison, but it is not an intervention trial — groups reflect physician-decided treatment. LVEDD values in the thrombolysis group (mean 24.4 mm) are unusually low (normal adult range ~37-53 mm), likely reflecting severe RV-mediated LV compression but should be noted as potentially extreme. Fibrinogen reported as median only without IQR. No long-term follow-up data reported — study captures only in-hospital period. The sPESI data in Table 2 reports mean±SD alongside medians. The paper is primarily a predictive/observational study of biomarkers for thrombolysis, not a treatment efficacy trial; caution is warranted in interpreting as evidence of thrombolysis efficacy.

summary: This single-center prospective observational study in Spain followed 1,966 patients (hospitalized and non-hospitalized) over 12 months after acute COVID-19 infection to identify risk factors for post-acute sequelae (PASC) and evaluate the impact of acute-phase treatments. Approximately one-third of patients developed PASC; female sex, obesity, asthma, and disease severity were independent risk factors. Among hospitalized patients, treatment with remdesivir was associated with significantly shorter median PASC symptom duration in both moderate disease (109 vs. 262 days) and severe disease (187 vs. 284 days), as was dexamethasone in moderate disease (133 vs. 271 days) and severe disease (266 vs. 309 days), while tocilizumab and methylprednisolone showed no significant benefit.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational prospective cohort study — not an RCT. Treatment assignment was by physician protocol based on disease severity (severe confounding by indication). The primary comparative analysis uses Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank tests for symptom duration, but exact log-rank p-values and hazard ratios are not reported in table form — only the median durations with IQRs are given in Table 6 and referenced in the text/figure caption. Arm IDs 1-8 represent the 4 treatment comparison pairs (remdesivir moderate, no-remdesivir moderate, remdesivir severe, no-remdesivir severe, dexamethasone moderate, no-dexamethasone moderate, dexamethasone severe, no-dexamethasone severe). Arm IDs 9-11 represent mild/moderate/severe disease severity groups for PASC prevalence. Arm IDs 12-13 represent non-PASC and PASC groups for biomarker outcomes. The tocilizumab/sarilumab and methylprednisolone/prednisone comparisons (Table 6) are not extracted as separate outcomes but described in subgroup analyses. Ns for tocilizumab arms: moderate No=466/Yes=49; severe No=193/Yes=139. Ns for methylprednisolone arms: moderate No=395/Yes=120; severe No=126/Yes=206. Kaplan-Meier curve data (Figure 2) provides additional tocilizumab and methylprednisolone median values but no formal HR or p-values are tabulated. Some lab values in Table 3 had unusual n discrepancy (1159+286=1445 but hospitalized total is 1733); this likely reflects that not all hospitalized patients had blood tests available.

summary: This matched cohort study compared 216 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors who received intravenous Remdesivir during acute infection to 216 matched controls who received no antiviral treatment, assessing post-COVID-19 pain at a mean of 18.4 months post-hospitalization. Remdesivir-treated patients had significantly lower prevalence of any chronic post-COVID-19 pain (22.7% vs. 39.8%; adjusted OR 0.444, 95% CI 0.292–0.674, p<0.001), with specific protection against thorax/chest (OR 0.277, p=0.01) and lumbar spine (OR 0.347, p=0.02) pain. Remdesivir was also associated with significantly lower rates of post-COVID-19 anxiety and depression, but had no effect on sleep quality.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The Remdesivir arm had 300 invited but only 216 participated; the paper does not detail selection of the control arm beyond matching criteria. Follow-up duration of 18.4 months used to calculate weeks (≈79.6 weeks). Adjusted ORs for pain locations other than thorax/chest and lumbar spine (cervical, shoulder, elbow-wrist, hip, knee) were not reported in multivariate form — only unadjusted p-values from Table 1 are available; these locations were omitted from outcomes to avoid redundancy but raw counts are: cervical (arm1: 3/216 1.4%, arm2: 4/216 1.8%, p=0.705), shoulder (arm1: 1/216 0.5%, arm2: 4/216 1.8%, p=0.178), elbow-wrist (arm1: 1/216 0.5%, arm2: 4/216 1.8%, p=0.178), hip (arm1: 2/216 0.9%, arm2: 4/216 1.8%, p=0.414), knee (arm1: 3/216 1.4%, arm2: 7/216 3.3%, p=0.206). The anxiety/depression OR values (0.039 and 0.057) are unusually large protective effects that appear driven by the very low event rates in the Remdesivir arm (4 and 7 cases respectively) — these are reported verbatim as stated. The paper mentions figure 1 shows pain location distribution but no additional numeric data beyond Table 1 was present in figures.

summary: This is an exploratory analysis of the SCORPIO-SR phase 3 RCT evaluating whether 5-day oral ensitrelvir (SARS-CoV-2 3CL protease inhibitor) given during acute mild-to-moderate COVID-19 reduces the subsequent risk of post-COVID condition (PCC) in 1,798 patients followed for up to 48 weeks. Using a stringent PCC definition (presence of symptoms plus failure to return to pre-COVID health), ensitrelvir 125 mg was associated with a trend toward reduced PCC risk at weeks 12, 24, and 48, with statistically significant relative risk reductions observed for neurological symptoms at some timepoints. However, no outcomes reached statistical significance for the primary broad PCC definitions, and the study was explicitly exploratory and post hoc, so results should be interpreted cautiously.

summary: This retrospective propensity-score-matched case-control study from Italy enrolled 737 adults with COVID-19 (January 2021–March 2022) to evaluate whether early treatment with monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) or antivirals reduced the risk of long COVID (defined as symptoms persisting ≥4 weeks). summary: This retrospective cohort study from Vietnam compared standard of care (SoC) alone versus SoC plus antivirals (predominantly molnupiravir) in 142 vaccinated adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 breakthrough infection. summary: This propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US EHR platform examined whether SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with reduced long COVID risk in 5,162 matched pairs of adults with type 2 diabetes who contracted COVID-19 between 2020-2024. SGLT2 inhibitor users had a significantly lower risk of developing long COVID over 12 months (HR=0.85, 95% CI 0.79-0.91), with particularly pronounced reductions in anxiety/depression (HR=0.73), headache (HR=0.56), cognitive symptoms (HR=0.69), pain (HR=0.84), and abdominal symptoms (HR=0.84); fatigue, chest pain, abnormal breathing, and myalgia were not significantly reduced. The protective association was consistent across age groups and sexes and was replicated in three sensitivity analyses comparing SGLT2i to DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Lung disease was associated with lower baseline FEV1 (-16.9%), FVC (-8.0%), and DLCO (-13.6%), but a faster DLCO recovery of +1.7%/month (95% CI 0.6-2.8, p=0.003). Restrictive disease had the lowest predicted PFT values across all measures.

summary: This retrospective cohort study of 405 post-COVID-19 patients attending a pulmonary clinic in Israel (February 2020–March 2021) compared long-term pulmonary function test (PFT) trajectories between 155 patients who received corticosteroids (CS) during acute COVID-19 and 250 who did not. Despite lower baseline FEV1 (-9.4%) and FVC (-12.3%), CS-treated patients recovered pulmonary function significantly faster (+0.9%/month FEV1, +0.85%/month FVC; both p=0.001), as shown by multivariable linear mixed-effects models adjusting for multiple confounders. The faster PFT recovery with CS was observed across all subgroups including those with BMI ≥30 and chronic lung disease, though substantial confounding by disease severity (CS-treated patients had 93% hospitalization rate vs. 20% in untreated) limits causal inference.

The baseline values reported in Table 1 reflect the FIRST clinic visit (mean 6.4 months post-COVID), not the time of acute infection. 3. summary: This retrospective observational cohort study used two large US EHR networks (N3C and PCORnet) to examine whether pre-existing metformin use in adults with diabetes or prediabetes was associated with a lower risk of developing post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC/long COVID) following COVID-19 infection. After IPTW weighting for baseline confounders, cumulative incidence of PASC (by U09.9 code) at 180 days was consistently lower in metformin-exposed versus comparator groups across both databases (e.g., N3C: 1.6% vs 2.0%; PCORnet: 1.28% vs 1.46%), and mortality was also lower in metformin users. Formal between-group hazard ratios or confidence intervals were not reported in this supplementary document; adjusted effect estimates are available in the primary manuscript.

summary: This propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX global EHR network evaluated molnupiravir (vs. no antiviral) in 9,421 matched pairs of non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients with pre-existing psychiatric disorders (psychotic, mood, or anxiety disorders) during the Omicron period (January 2022–May 2023). Molnupiravir was associated with a 24% reduction in the risk of all-cause hospitalization or death within 30 days (HR 0.760, 95% CI 0.665–0.869, p<0.001). At 1-year follow-up, molnupiravir-treated patients had significantly lower rates of 9 post-COVID-19 conditions including fatigue (HR 0.718), cognitive symptoms (HR 0.769), chest/throat pain (HR 0.615), myalgia (HR 0.647), and palpitation (HR 0.641), all statistically significant.

summary: This propensity-score matched cohort study from the multicenter HOPE-2 registry examined the effect of corticosteroid therapy during acute COVID-19 hospitalization on 18-month all-cause mortality and long-term symptoms in 796 patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Corticosteroid use was not associated with differences in 18-month all-cause mortality (44.0% vs. 39.7%, log-rank p=0.52) or in-hospital mortality (41.2% vs. 36.4%, p=0.167), and no significant differences were found in any long-term post-COVID-19 symptom except for a higher rate of clinically relevant bleeding events in the corticosteroid group (4.1% vs. 0%, p=0.029). However, corticosteroid-treated patients had significantly shorter hospital stays (median 8 vs. 11 days, p<0.001), suggesting a possible benefit in recovery time without clear long-term benefit or harm in this high-risk cardiac subpopulation.

summary: This uncontrolled single-arm prospective observational study enrolled 183 adults with acute PCR-confirmed COVID-19 (Feb 2020–Jun 2022) from multiple countries, and evaluated a multi-component protocol including probiotics, vitamins D/C/E, zinc, selenium, glutathione, N-acetylcysteine, quercetin, and a low-carbohydrate diet, with pain killers as the only permitted medication. COVID symptom scores decreased significantly from a mean of 7.66 (SD 1.26) at baseline to 6.39 (SD 1.12) at 72 hours (p<0.005), with a regression-modeled daily reduction of 0.97 score points (R²=0.97, p<0.0001); overall median recovery was 13 days, shorter than historical comparators of 12–21 days. The study had no control group and was primarily aimed at preventing long COVID rather than treating it; the authors reported no long-term post-COVID complications at 6-month follow-up, but this claim cannot be evaluated without a comparator group.

summary: This nationwide retrospective propensity-score-matched cohort study in South Korea examined whether oral antiviral treatment (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or molnupiravir) during acute COVID-19 reduces the risk of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) in adults aged ≥60 years diagnosed during the 2022 Omicron wave. Among 957,036 matched pairs for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and 243,360 matched pairs for molnupiravir, both antivirals were significantly associated with reduced incidence of multiple PASC outcomes (cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, neurological, gastrointestinal, and metabolic) between 30 and 120 days post-diagnosis, with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir showing broader and larger risk reductions (e.g., aHR 0.57 for new dialysis) compared to molnupiravir.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Full numeric data for all 27 PASC outcomes across both cohorts are in Tables 2 and 3 (not available in this text excerpt — supplementary tables eTables 3-30 also not available). The asthma nirmatrelvir/ritonavir CI (0.83-0.94) appears internally inconsistent with the stated aHR of 0.98 — this may be a typographical error in the paper; values extracted verbatim. The acute renal failure CI (0.78-0.82) is also inconsistent with aHR 0.85 — likely a transcription error in the paper text; extracted verbatim. Per-arm event counts and raw rates were not reported in the available text. summary: This Finnish randomized controlled trial (SOLIDARITY Finland) tested remdesivir (5-day course) plus standard of care versus standard of care alone in 208 adults hospitalized for COVID-19, following them for one year to assess long COVID outcomes. At one year, self-reported recovery was nearly identical between groups (85% remdesivir vs 86% standard of care; RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.47–1.90), with no statistically significant differences in exertional dyspnea, fatigue, quality of life, or any of 21 long COVID symptoms. Regardless of treatment, long COVID burden was substantial: roughly one in four survivors reported major bother from fatigue, and one in six reported poor overall recovery.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an RCT sub-study focusing on 3-month pulmonary sequelae. The comparator structure is complex: remdesivir (n=16) vs its SoC (n=27); HCQ (n=40) vs its SoC (n=47). Some SoC participants served as control for both drugs simultaneously, so n=108 total does not equal sum of all subgroups. Arm 3 (SoC) represents the combined SoC pool; per-arm SoC group sizes differ by comparison (n=27 for remdesivir; n=47 for HCQ). The overall total population n=108 is used for biomarker and CT prevalence analyses. Biomarker outcomes (MMP-9, VEGF-A, SP-D, TIMP-2) are reported for the full cohort vs healthy controls (n=24) — healthy controls coded as arm_id=4 and full patient cohort as arm_id=5 for biomarker outcomes. IQR values for biomarkers not reported (medians only from figure caption). Reversible CT findings in Table 3 arm 1 vs arm 3 comparison shows 3 (18.8%) vs 4 (14.8%) but uses n values from remdesivir comparison. The coefficient estimate CIs for FEV1 comparisons appear to be t-statistics or standardised, not raw mean differences — reported verbatim as stated. KCO results also extracted in Table 2 but not given separate outcome object due to space — overall: median 97.4% (IQR 84.1–107.0); remdesivir 96.1 (78.1–99.8), HCQ 102.0 (92.0–108.0), SoC 92.8 (79.4–107.0). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is not a long COVID treatment trial per se; it is a pre-specified exploratory analysis of long-term symptom outcomes from an acute COVID-19 treatment RCT (NOR-Solidarity). Treatment was given during acute hospitalization, and PROMs were collected at 1 and 3 months post-randomization. The between-group mean differences in Table 2 appear to use the convention remdesivir minus control (negative values indicate worse scores for remdesivir on CAT where higher=worse, and positive values indicate better scores for remdesivir on SF-36/EQ-5D where higher=better). The n_analyzed values are set to randomized N (42 and 76) as the full analysis set with multiple imputation was used. Actual completers were 27/42 and 53/76 for the 3-month CAT. Adverse event data were not reported in this paper; they were reported in the primary publication (Barratt-Due et al. 2021). Remdesivir dose and duration details not provided in this paper. Sensitivity analysis numeric results are in supplementary materials not available in the extracted text, but authors state they showed even stronger indications of lack of benefit.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a large retrospective EHR cohort study using propensity score matching (1:1), NOT a treatment trial. The 'intervention' is prior COVID-19 vaccination (any brand/type), and outcomes are PASC symptoms and new diagnoses at 28 and 90 days post-COVID-19 diagnosis. Per-arm denominators for condition-specific outcomes (hypertension, diabetes, etc.) vary because patients with pre-existing conditions are excluded from those specific analyses — exact per-arm denominators for sub-analyses are not reported (only total N for the outcome row is given in Table 2/3 as 'Total, No.' which appears to be the combined eligible population for that outcome). Rates reported as per 1000 were converted to percentages by dividing by 10. The 28-day and 90-day outcomes for the same condition are treated as separate outcomes (different timepoints, different outcome IDs) due to the study design measuring cumulative incidence separately. No vaccine type, dose, or brand information is reported. Attributable risk (risk difference) per 1000 is also reported in the paper tables but was not separately extracted as between-group effects since RR is the primary reported measure.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an interrupted time series (ITS) observational study, not a conventional intervention trial with separate arms. The study uses a self-as-control design: participants serve as their own pre-vaccination comparators. All effect estimates are expressed as percentage change in odds (from logistic regression on logit scale), not as absolute mean differences or standard ORs. Key estimates: pre-vaccination trajectory -0.3%/week (OR 0.997, 95% CI 0.991-1.002, p=0.25); first dose level change OR 0.872 (95% CI 0.814-0.934, p<0.001), i.e. -12.8%; slope change after first dose +0.3%/week (OR 1.006, 95% CI 0.996-1.016, p=0.51); second dose level change OR 0.912 (95% CI 0.859-0.969, p=0.003), i.e. -8.8%; slope change after second dose -0.8%/week (OR 0.989, 95% CI 0.979-0.999, p<0.001 per week). Activity-limiting: first dose OR 0.877 (0.805-0.955, p=0.003); second dose OR 0.909 (0.844-0.979, p=0.01). Individual symptom data appear primarily in Fig 4 with only selected values in text; data for 10 symptoms (weakness/tiredness, loss of smell, shortness of breath, loss of taste, headache, trouble sleeping, difficulty concentrating, muscle ache, worry/anxiety, memory loss/confusion) and >3 and >5 symptom composites exist as modelled probabilities in figure only — detailed per-symptom CIs are in supplementary table 6 (not reproduced in main text). Per-arm raw means/SDs are not available; this design produces only trajectory parameters. Follow-up: median 219 days (31.3 weeks) from study start to end; median 67 days (9.6 weeks) post second dose. Time since infection at final visit: mean 308.9 days (SD 129.0).

summary: This retrospective follow-up study of 1,236 Iranian adults hospitalized for COVID-19 who had previously reported long-COVID symptoms compared the persistence of symptoms (>1 year, termed 'long long-COVID') between vaccinated (n=1,185) and unvaccinated (n=51) individuals. Vaccination with any COVID-19 vaccine was significantly associated with higher odds of persistent long-COVID symptoms at follow-up (44.6% vs. 29.4%; adjusted OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.06–3.63, p=0.032). The study is observational with a very small unvaccinated comparator group and serious confounding risk, limiting causal inference; the authors nonetheless strongly recommend vaccination given its well-established protection against severe disease and death.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational retrospective cohort, not an intervention trial. The 'intervention' is COVID-19 vaccination (self-selected, not randomized). The unvaccinated comparator group is very small (n=51), limiting statistical power for individual symptom comparisons. Table 1 reports p-values for individual symptoms but no ORs per symptom — p-values extracted as chi-square results. Several symptoms had zero events in unvaccinated group (muscle pain, chest pain, palpitation, loss of taste, sore throat, dizziness, concentration difficulty, diarrhea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite) — no p-value calculable for these (listed as '-' in paper). Remaining secondary symptom outcomes with p-values reported: cough (p=0.497), excess sputum (p=0.942), headache (p=0.679), excess sweating (p=0.667) — omitted from outcomes array for brevity but all showed non-significance. Follow-up duration estimated as ~17 months (mean reported as 16.8–17.1 months) converted to ~74 weeks.

summary: This 1-year follow-up study examined whether intravenous human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell (hUC-MSC) therapy, given during acute severe COVID-19, reduced long-term post-infection sequelae compared to standard treatment alone in 25 discharged patients (8 hUC-MSC, 17 controls). The primary finding was that fatigue remained common overall (60%), but only 25% of the hUC-MSC group reported persistent fatigue at 1 year compared to 76.5% of controls (p=0.028); the hUC-MSC group also had significantly lower KL-6 levels (2585.5 vs 3120.7 U/ml, p<0.001) and lower MDA levels (9.27 vs 9.91 nmol/ml, p=0.036), suggesting reduced lung injury and oxidative stress. No serious adverse events were attributable to hUC-MSC therapy at 1 year, though the study is severely limited by its very small sample size, single-centre design, and non-randomised follow-up attrition.

trial_rating.result_basis: Fatigue rate 25% (2/8) in hUC-MSC group vs 76.5% (13/17) in control group at 1-year follow-up, p=0.028.

summary: The Metcovid trial tested whether a 5-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone (0.5 mg/kg twice daily) given during acute COVID-19 hospitalization affected lung function 120 days later in adult patients with oxygen saturation ≤94% or requiring ventilation. Among 118 survivors who completed pulmonary function testing, those who received methylprednisolone had higher forced vital capacity (FVC: 3.2 L vs. 2.9 L, p=0.01), which remained significant after adjusting for mechanical ventilation use and baseline inflammation levels; forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) was also higher in the methylprednisolone group in univariate analysis (2.6 L vs. 2.3 L, p=0.01) but not after adjustment. A key caveat is that this was an exploratory secondary analysis of a trial not powered for lung function outcomes, the methylprednisolone group had higher baseline inflammation (IL-6) and more severe initial disease, and only 118 of 246 eligible survivors completed adequate testing, limiting the reliability of the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: FVC 3.2 L (MP) vs. 2.9 L (placebo), p=0.01 in multivariate analysis; Cohen's d=0.37 (moderate effect size); FEV1 significant only in univariate analysis (p=0.01), not multivariate (p=0.12).

This study is not a traditional long COVID treatment trial — it is a target trial emulation study examining antiviral treatment effects on cardiovascular post-acute sequelae in HOSPITALIZED COVID-19 patients. summary: This retrospective observational study compared SLAB51 probiotic supplementation (2,400 billion bacteria/day) during hospitalization versus standard care alone in 58 patients hospitalized for acute COVID-19 in Rome, Italy in early 2020. At 6 months post-discharge, fatigue (FAS >= 22) was significantly less prevalent in the probiotic group than the standard care group (41.7% vs 91.2%, p<0.01), and fatigued patients who received probiotics had significantly lower FAS scores (median 24 vs 34, p=0.02). As a non-randomized observational study where probiotic allocation was based on presence of intestinal symptoms rather than random assignment, these results are hypothesis-generating and subject to substantial confounding.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective observational study, NOT an RCT — allocation was based on clinical indication (intestinal symptoms) not randomization. Metabolomic data (Arginine, Asparagine, Lactate, 3-Hydroxyisobutyrate) are reported only in figures (Figure 1A-D) with no numeric values in text or tables — only directional significance statements are provided. Treatment duration was estimated as the median hospitalization period (~3 weeks for OB+ group: median 23 days). The paper does not report exact p-values for metabolomic comparisons, only that they were statistically significant. FAS overall score among ALL 58 patients reported as fatigued median 32 (IQR 26-36) and non-fatigued 20 (IQR 17-20), p<0.01. The n_analyzed for FAS scores among fatigued subgroup is 10 (OB+) and 31 (OB-) based on the reported fatigue prevalence counts. ICU sub-analysis FAS scores reported with reversed IQR notation in text (OB+ '24 (26-22)') — likely a typo for 22-26.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a prevention trial (metformin during acute COVID-19 to prevent long COVID), not a treatment trial of established long COVID. The trial used a Bayesian framework; 95% CrI (credible intervals) reported rather than frequentist CIs. Table 3 reports model-based marginal risk estimates with 95% CrI for each arm — these are the per-arm model-estimated risks (not raw proportions). Raw observed counts from Table 2 were also extracted. The Table 3 note indicates 'PASCD' primary outcome rows are covariate-adjusted while secondary PASCD and clinician diagnosis rows are unadjusted; outcome IDs 1 (adjusted primary) and 2 (unadjusted PASCD) both included. Note that observed events for PASCD day 90 in Table 2 show 52 for placebo but in text says 51 — Table 2 used (52). The risk ratio for PASCD primary outcome (0.79, 95% CrI 0.474-1.230) is reported in the abstract but not in Table 3; it is included in Figure 2. The adjusted risk ratio for clinician-diagnosed long COVID day 180 is reported as 0.50 (95% CrI 0.16-0.99) in text and 0.495 (95% CrI 0.155-0.995) in abstract — both are extracted under outcome 3. Symptom burden odds ratios extracted from Table 3; per-arm ordinal data not reported numerically. PPE (posterior probability of efficacy) values: primary PASCD day 180=0.83; PASCD day 90=0.66 (adjusted), day 120=0.93 (adjusted); clinician LC day 120=0.63, day 180=0.96; symptom burden OR day 90 PPE=0.69, day 120 PPE=0.98, day 180 PPE=0.74.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Substantial residual confounding likely despite propensity score matching: favipiravir recipients were older, more severely ill (longer symptom duration, more oxygen supplementation, more hospitalization), and received more co-medications, meaning the treatment groups differed systematically in disease severity and care intensity.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Patients living alone had significantly higher risk of anhedonia (aOR 2.253, 95% CI 1.329–3.818, p=0.003).
158 (44.4%) received favipiravir <24h, 125 (35.1%) within 24-72h, and 73 (20.5%) >72h after diagnosis; timing-specific effects on depression not reported separately.

summary: This propensity score-matched longitudinal cohort study from Indonesia examined whether favipiravir (an antiviral given during acute COVID-19) reduced the incidence of post-COVID depression in 712 participants followed biweekly for 60 days. Depression occurred in 16.0% of favipiravir recipients versus 21.1% of non-recipients; after adjustment for multiple confounders using Cox regression, favipiravir was associated with a significantly lower hazard of post-COVID depression (aHR 0.488, 95% CI 0.339–0.701, p<0.001). Favipiravir showed specific protective effects against depressive mood (aHR 0.378) and anhedonia (aHR 0.543), but not sleep disorders, concentration disturbance, or fatigue; living alone was independently associated with greater anhedonia risk.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. 1) The paper uses Cox regression and reports adjusted estimates labeled as 'aOR' in the text and 'Exp(B)' in Table 3, but since it uses Cox regression, these are properly hazard ratios (aHR), not odds ratios — extracted as adjusted_hazard_ratio accordingly. 2) Per-arm sample sizes (356 per arm) are inferred from the 1:1 matching of 712 total participants and the reported depression event counts (57/356 favipiravir, 75/356 non-favipiravir). 3) Symptom-specific PHQ-9 subscale analyses for sleep disorders (S7 Table), concentration (S8 Table), and fatigue (S9 Table) are referenced as supplementary tables but no numeric estimates are provided in the main text; only depressive mood and anhedonia HR values are in the main text. 4) No per-arm means/SDs for PHQ-9 total scores are reported — only binary event counts and HRs. 5) Vaccination percentage of 52.5% for favipiravir arm and 47.5% for non-favipiravir arm represents those NOT infected within 14 days of second vaccine dose (i.e., vaccine-protected group).
